title: About
text:
Thomas Lund Koch




I am an evolutionary biologist interested in how bioactive peptides, including neuropeptides, hormones, and toxins, evolve and shape interactions between organisms.
Recently, my work has focused on how peptides mediate interactions such as venom use, parasitism, host–pathogen interactions, symbiosis, and sexual interactions, with a particular emphasis on molecular mimicry. I combine fieldwork, comparative genomics, computational biology, and physiological testing.
I am currently a Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral fellow at the University of Oslo, where I study the origin and loss of venom in marine snails.
My broader aim is to understand how evolutionary processes generate molecular innovations and how these innovations influence ecological interactions.

title: About
text:
Research approach
I enjoy research that connects organismal biology and natural history with molecular and genomic approaches. I am particularly interested in questions that can be addressed by combining broad evolutionary comparisons with targeted functional experiments.

title: The evolution of peptide signaling systems
text:
Bessegen, Norway
Peptide hormones and neuropeptides are widespread regulators of animal physiology and behavior.
I use comparative approaches to reconstruct the origins and diversification of peptide-encoding genes across animal lineages, and to connect evolutionary hypotheses with functional characterization.

title: The evolution of peptide signaling systems
text:
Research directions

Identify peptide-encoding genes across diverse animal genomes.
Reconstruct the evolutionary histories of peptide families and their receptors.
Investigate lineage-specific gene expansions and potential functional innovation.
Use evolutionary predictions to guide ligand discovery and receptor deorphanization.


Methods
Genome mining · Comparative genomics · Phylogenetics · Peptide synthesis · Receptor deorphanization

title: Research
text: My research asks how bioactive peptides and their receptors evolve and how they control physiology. I am particularly interested the cases of molecular mimicry, where one organism can control the physiology of its target. I combine fieldwork, comparative genomics, computational biology, and physiological testing to trace the origins and diversification of diverse molecular systems.

title: Research
text:
Venom evolution
Venoms have evolved independently across many animal lineages, often recruiting molecules that originally served other physiological roles. In cone snails, I study how a venom system with hundreds of toxins arises and diversifies, and how it responds to ecological change.
Key questions I investigate:

Where do toxins come from, and why are some proteins repeatedly recruited into venom?
How do shifts in ecology, e.g. diet, reshape venom composition?
How do gene duplication, regulatory change, and sequence evolution contribute to evolutionary innovation?

Our work has for instance shown that prey shifts drive venom evolution in cone snails and have traced many cone snail toxins back to ancestral neuropeptides and hormones. My current work at the University of Oslo uses comparative genomics to investigate the origin and loss of venom across marine snails.
Explore the venom evolution projects →

title: Research
text:
Evolution of peptide signaling
Peptide hormones and neuropeptides are ancient, diverse signaling molecules found in multicellular organism from animals to plants. Their evolutionary histories show how communication systems originate, expand, and acquire new functions across animal lineages.
Key questions I investigate:

How old are the major families of peptide-encoding genes?
How do duplication and loss shape the diversity of signaling systems, from cnidarians to bilaterians?
How can toxins and evolutionary analyses guide the discovery of previously unknown peptide ligands?

I began this work with genome-wide surveys of neuropeptide genes in cnidarians and placozoans. More recently, I have used the toxins of cone snails to reconstruct the origins of the somatostatin and allatostatin-C, and to build a toxin-based approach to neuropeptide discovery. We are also developing machine-learning methods to predict neuropeptide precursors from protein sequences.
Explore the peptide signaling project →

title: Research
text:
Molecular mimicry and host manipulation
Organisms can manipulate one another by producing molecules that imitate endogenous signaling peptides. We call these molecules doppelgänger peptides. They are found in venoms, parasites, and pathogens, and they let one species hijack the signaling pathways of another.
Key questions I investigate:

How often do interacting organisms evolve molecular mimics, and in which lineages?
What evolutionary processes allow a mimic to activate a host receptor?
How do mimics help animals paralyze, defend against, or manipulate other organisms?
Can comparative genomics reveal the origins and spread of mimicry?

Examples from our work include somatostatin and insulin mimics that disrupt blood glucose in the prey of a fish-hunting cone snail, neurotensin mimics produced by intestinal hookworms, and bradykinin mimics that evolved repeatedly as defensive toxins. We reviewed the field in Trends in Biochemical Sciences and General and Comparative Endocrinology.
Explore the molecular mimicry project →

title: Research
text:
From evolution to application
Toxins and mimics have been refined by evolution to act on specific receptors, which makes them useful starting points for drug discovery. We are working on several potential drug leads inspired by nature.
See publications →

title: Molecular mimicry in biological interactions
text:
Plants and parasites have intricate evolutionary relationships.
Organisms do not interact only through behavior and ecology. They also interact through molecules. Venomous animals, parasites, and pathogens can produce molecules that resemble target signaling molecules, allowing them to manipulate the target’s physiology and development.
I am interested in the evolution of these molecular strategies, particularly the mimicry of peptide hormones and other signaling molecules.

title: Molecular mimicry in biological interactions
text:
Research directions

Identify candidate peptide mimics in interacting organisms.
Investigate their evolutionary origins and patterns of diversification.
Test whether candidate mimics activate host receptors or signaling pathways.


Methods
Comparative genomics · Secretome analysis · Peptide synthesis · Receptor pharmacology · Functional signaling assays
